title: Har Ki Dun Trek: 7 Days in the Valley of the Gods, Uttarakhand
meta_title: Har Ki Dun Trek 7 Days from Dehradun | Blue Diamond Voyage
meta_description: 7-day Har Ki Dun trek from Dehradun via Sankri, Taluka and Osla village: Swargarohini views, Marinda Tal, camps, guide, cook and all veg meals.
tagline: Wooden villages, birch forests and the peaks the Pandavas climbed to heaven
facts: April to June, September to November
intro: Har Ki Dun is one of the gentlest high-Himalayan treks in India and one of the most beautiful. From the road head at Sankri you walk up the Supin River through walnut, pine and cedar, past the old wooden village of Osla, to a broad meadow facing Swargarohini, the 'stairway to heaven' of the Mahabharata. A professional trek leader, cook and support team look after the camps, and all meals are vegetarian. It suits fit first-time trekkers aged about 12 and up.
highlights: Views of Swargarohini, Black Peak (Kalanag) and Bandarpoonch
Osla village, with its carved wooden houses and the Someshwar temple
Meadows, pine, cedar and Himalayan birch forest along the Supin River
The Har Ki Dun valley, linked in legend to the Pandavas' last journey
Marinda Tal, a quiet lake below the peaks
Two nights in Sankri, a village with views of the Swargarohini range

best_time: April to June for rhododendrons and long days; September to November for the clearest views after the monsoon. Avoid July and August (landslides). In December to March the upper trail is under snow and only experienced winter trekkers should go.
seasons: Days about 15° to 20°, nights near freezing at Kalkatiyadhar. Rhododendrons in April.
Crisp and clear, nights below freezing from late October.
Monsoon rain and landslides on the road to Sankri.

faqs.q: How fit do I need to be for Har Ki Dun?
faqs.a: You should be able to walk 5 to 7 hours a day with a light daypack. Start walking or climbing stairs daily for a month before the trek. Children from about 12 can do it with a parent.
Yes, all meals on this trek are vegetarian. Tell us if you need Jain food: the cook can leave out onion, garlic and potato with notice.
Signal is weak in Sankri and there is none on most of the trail. Tell your family you will be out of reach for four days.
The highest point is about 3,560 m. The climb is gradual, but headaches can happen. Your trek leader checks oxygen levels every evening and will bring you down if needed.

good_to_know.title: Packing for the trek
good_to_know.text: Trekking shoes with ankle support, a warm down jacket, thermals, a rain jacket, cap, gloves, a 30 to 40 litre daypack, two water bottles, sunscreen and a head torch. Nights are cold even in June.

good_to_know.title: Leave no trace
good_to_know.text: Carry all plastic back down. The valley is part of Govind Wildlife Sanctuary, and camping in the Har Ki Dun meadow itself is not allowed.

good_to_know.title: UPI, cards and cash
good_to_know.text: UPI works almost everywhere, even at small stalls. Keep some cash in INR 100 and 200 notes for temples, parking, tips and places where the network is weak.

good_to_know.title: Temple and shrine etiquette
good_to_know.text: Cover shoulders and knees. Remove shoes where asked, and carry socks for hot stone floors. Leather belts and bags are not allowed inside some Jain and Hindu temples. Ask before photographing people and inside shrines.

good_to_know.title: Water and street food
good_to_know.text: Drink sealed bottled or filtered water only. Choose busy stalls where food is cooked in front of you, and skip cut fruit and ice from roadside stalls.

good_to_know.title: Driving times
good_to_know.text: Indian roads are slower than the kilometres suggest: plan on 40 to 50 km an hour on highways and much less in hills and towns. Your driver's breaks and meal stops are built into the timings.

good_to_know.title: Plugs and tipping
good_to_know.text: Plugs are Indian three-pin and two-pin, 230 volts. Tipping drivers and guides about INR 300 to 500 a day is appreciated.

dining_intro: India is the easiest country in the world for vegetarian and Jain travellers. We send your dietary brief to every hotel, and your driver knows clean, pure-vegetarian restaurants on each road day.
dining_avoid: Ask for food cooked fresh and tell the kitchen clearly if you eat Jain: no onion, garlic, ginger, potato or other root vegetables. Many dishes start with an onion-garlic base even when the menu says vegetarian.
food_card: Hum shuddh shakahari (Jain) hain. Pyaz, lahsun, adrak, aloo, gajar ya koi bhi zameen ke neeche ki sabzi nahi. Ande nahi. Kripya taaza banaiye. Dhanyavaad.
